Also - changing distros won't change this. I'd like to clear a few things up, since I see a lot of Linux Distro wars.

Linux is a kernel - a guy named Linus maintains the kernel. The kernel is simply the software layer that stands between the hardware and the applications.

GNU - is a free software repository. The software from GNU and a number of other free software repositories (although GNU is the main one) are used to run on the kernel.

The difference between distros, is simply the free software that is packaged in the default build. You can add or remove any of it via whatever packaging system comes with your distribution (apt-get or yum usually). So, if you don't like your windows manager for instance, you can install another one.

The point is, it doesn't really matter what distribution you use. You're still likely going to have to add or remove some amount of software to make it how you want. None of the distros have a superty-duperty advantage over the others. They seriously just package up slightly different stuff

You are not at all expecting too much. I would like to point out a few things though.

  1. Linux is not Windows. It does not want to be Windows. It does not attempt to emulate Windows. It's goal is not to be easy for Windows users to switch to. Linux can help you accomplish the same things as Windows, but it may (and often times will) take a radically different approach. If you are a Windows user, that approach may not be intuitive to you. It may seem harder. It may seem like more work. However, you probably grew up on Windows. And it, like your first language, has become easy and the norm for you. The fact that Linux is different does not mean it is worse. Don't get caught up in trying to replicate details of Windows. Here's an embarrassing example of my own from when I first switched to Linux. I wanted to get on IRC and MIRC was the way to do that in Windows, so I search "MIRC linux". Sure enough I get a bunch of hits telling me that I need to install WINE and do XYZ to get MIRC running on Linux. After installing WINE I tweak my way around until I get a usable MIRC. At this point I've got a mock Windows registry on my system and think "Gosh, this Linux think is so complicated". What was wrong with my approach was I took the Windows solution and tried to convert it to Linux, instead of just searching for a Linux solution. Whenever I hear someone say they are trying to install flash, java, google chrome, on Linux, I always wonder if they really want those things, or if they are just trying to convert a Windows way of doing something. I've been on Debian for a year and have not once specifically needed any of those things. Yeah sure, java-common is installed on my machine, but I never had to bother installing it specifically, it was installed automatically because a program actually needed it.

  2. If you want to use Linux, don't dual boot. Like learning a new language, you need to immerse yourself in the culture to really get it. I tried dual booting over and over again. I was never able to learn to use my Linux system because the moment anything was different than Windows and I didn't know what to do, I would just switch over to Windows and do it "the old fashioned way". Don't use Windows as a crutch. Learn to walk in Linux. Learn to solve problems in Linux.

  3. Don't blame Linux for for software/hardware/driver problems. The most notorious example is of course graphics drivers on Linux. They are slower than their Windows counterpart, they require some shoddy installation that may trash your entire system, and sometimes they just don't work. Don't for even one second blame this on Linux. Graphics drivers sucking on Linux is not because Linux sucks, but because graphics companies suck. The hardware manufacturers make proprietary closed source hardware. The fact that hackers have been able to reverse engineer and make open source drivers that work at all is astonishing. Sometimes manufacturers put out closed source drivers for Linux, but these were written by people who are Windows people, who don't know the kernel, and who view Linux as the minority that they have to support out of political correctness. They don't care about Linux customers. Sometimes Microsoft even pays companies to NOT support Linux in their software projects. This goes back to point (2.), instead of saying "Windows supports X, and I use X on Windows, but Linux doesn't support X, so I'll stay with Windows", just use Linux anyway and if your problem doesn't have a solution on Linux, then complain to the hardware manufacturers that need to change that you want Linux support. Or better yet, take the $100 you were going to burn on a new Windows license and donate it to an open source project that is trying to solve the problem you have. Get people to use Linux for Linux, and then when there are enough people on Linux for profiteers to care about them, they will start caring.

  • The Bundesliga returns on Friday, and as is traditional, the champions kick it off with the only Friday game of the weekend. Bayern will begin their quest for an unprecedented fourth straight title against the un-relegatable Hamburger SV.

  • Things didn't go really well for Hamburg in the Pokal, they fell behind twice to Carl Zeiss Jena only to equalize in each instance. The fourth-tier side came out on top in that fixture after nabbing a winner in the second half of extra time.

  • Pep Guardiola will be spoiled for choice in many positions, with Bayern having been bolstered by the return of Thiago Alcantara and Sebastian Rode to team training this week. Javi Martinez, Franck Ribéry, Holger Badstuber and Jan Kirchhoff will all miss the Hamburg match as they rehabilitate their respective injuries, while Sinan Kurt, Gianluca Gaudino and Julian Green are expected to play with the reserves this weekend.

  • Lahm: “If we're hungry, if we want it and have the energy, no other team will be German champions.”

  • Boateng: “Everyone says it's going to be easy, but HSV come here with nothing to lose. You must never underestimate your opponents.”

  • Hamburg is coached by Bruno Labbadia, who used to play for Bayern. He coached Stuttgart against Bayern during the 2013 Pokal final.

  • On the eve of the Bundesliga restart, Guardiola heaped special praise on the four summer signings. “I’m happy and highly motivated” Guardiola declared, a feeling shared by Rummenigge: “We’ve brought in very sensible reinforcements. I believe we can be very optimistic about the new season. I’d like us to start with a win.”
